Model assumptions

Particles drift with uniform cabin airflow u and mix through a random walk. Each component of ξ is independently standard normal. The illustrative mixing coefficient is 0.012 m²/s. The detector samples particles within a 0.25 m radius. The 6 m cabin geometry and detector sampling radius are illustrative. This model uses passive particles in microgravity and estimates transport only. It omits flame chemistry, cabin obstructions and detector response thresholds.

Ready to scan.

Map rows show distance across the cabin. Columns show distance along it. Each tile gives the percentage of runs sampled by the deadline. Select a tile for its results.

Ranked by sampling frequency, then median arrival among runs that met the deadline. The trials share scenario inputs across candidates. Results describe this simplified airflow model and depend on the rack layouts and smoke releases tested.

Arrival statistics use trials with at least one particle sampled. Each pair shares a random seed so that detector placement is the only change. The rack model uses prescribed flow deflection, a slower wake, and a solid obstacle at the rack. The heat map shows a horizontal slice through the cabin. It illustrates how a layout can affect sampling outcomes. Quantitative design predictions would require validated CFD or experiments. Particle arrival is a model result. A real lunar habitat test would need its cabin geometry, ventilation layout, and detector response.

Analytical transport model

When does smoke reach the detector plane?

Change the ventilation slider above to compare drift and mixing along the cabin axis.

Péclet numberPe = UL/D—
Most likely plane crossingtmode = L² / [√(9D² + U²L²) + 3D]—
Mean plane crossingE[T] = L/U for U > 0—
Richardson number · buoyancy vs. fanRi = gβΔTL / U²—
Particle settling speedvs = (ρp − ρg)gdp²Cc / (18μ)—

Slip correction

Cc = 1 + (2λ/dp)[1.257 + 0.4 exp(−1.1dp / 2λ)]

Ri uses a local 0.10 m plume length, a 30 K temperature difference and β ≈ 1/(293 K). Values much smaller than 1 favor forced flow. Values much larger than 1 indicate buoyancy may dominate. With the fan off, the ratio is undefined.

The animation adds downward settling to the passive particles. Ri is a diagnostic for warm gas, whose buoyant rise is outside this particle model. Settling assumes spherical particles of density 1,000 kg/m³ in room-temperature air near 1 atm. Values above a few micrometres let you explore larger illustrative particles. The model reflects particles at the walls and omits deposition. The plane-crossing formulas remain a one-dimensional axial reference.

NASA gravity values → · Stokes settling and slip correction →

First-passage time distribution

f(t)=L4πDt3exp(−(L−Ut)24Dt)

Here L is the axial distance to the detector plane, U is airflow speed and D is the effective mixing coefficient. The density f(t) describes one particle’s first crossing of an infinite plane in an unbounded one-dimensional drift–diffusion model. The 3D simulator uses a small sampling zone, cabin walls and multiple particles. Its first sampled particle is a different quantity. Moving the detector sideways changes the 3D sampling geometry while the axial plane remains in place.

Redner, A Guide to First-Passage Processes →

How to read the simulation

  1. Start with Ventilated cabin. The orange source releases simulated smoke for the first 8 seconds of model time. The arrows show the direction of airflow.
  2. Watch the blue detector. The first particle to enter its sampling zone sets the First particle arrival time. The counter counts each sampled particle once. Playback is twice as fast as model time.
  3. Try No directed ventilation or Detector near the wall. Compare the readouts after the same 60-second model interval.

The demo illustrates smoke transport in a simplified microgravity cabin. Detector sampling is a model event. A real alarm also depends on its sensor, threshold, and cabin conditions.

Combustion and transport

Physics lab

Explore a flame-sheet model, then see how a real flight experiment departs from its assumptions.

Idealized model

Burke–Schumann flame sheet

Fuel and oxygen enter separately. With infinitely fast chemistry, the reaction sits at the mixture fraction where just enough oxygen reaches the fuel.

C7H16 + 11 O2 → 7 CO2 + 8 H2O
s = 11MO₂ / Mfuel
Zst = YO₂,ox / (sYF,f + YO₂,ox)

Fuel and oxygen profiles

Z is the mass fraction of material originating in the pure-fuel stream. Y is a species mass fraction. The oxidizer oxygen mass fraction is xMO₂ / [xMO₂ + (1−x)MN₂], where x is the slider value as a fraction.

YF = max(0, (Z − Zst)/(1 − Zst))
YO₂ = YO₂,ox max(0, 1 − Z/Zst)

The model assumes pure heptane vapor, an O₂/N₂ oxidizer, equal species diffusivities and one infinitely fast overall reaction. Zst describes a mixture composition. Physical flame location requires a spatial mixing field. Extinction and cool-flame chemistry require finite-rate models.

Flame-sheet derivation, eqs. 31–33 →

NASA flight experiment

FLEX-500 · Heptane droplet

NASA reported two mean burning rates and the droplet diameters at hot- and cool-stage extinction.

d²(t) ≈ dstart² − K(t − tstart)
Δt ≈ (dstart² − dend²) / K
StageStart → end (mm)K (mm²/s)Est. time (s)

Times are calculated for consecutive idealized stages. NASA’s slide reports the endpoints and average slopes. This single run does not establish a general extinction time.

NASA FLEX-500 flight summary →

From flame sheet to flame strain

Scalar dissipation rate

The Burke–Schumann model finds the mixture composition at the flame sheet. Scalar dissipation measures how quickly diffusion erases composition differences there.

χ = 2D |∇Z|²
For a linear mixing layer, χ = 2D (ΔZ/δ)²

Illustration with ΔZ = 1 and constant molecular diffusivity D = 2 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s. This is an assumed value, separate from the simulator’s effective smoke mixing coefficient. Halving the thickness quadruples χ. In a real flamelet, evaluate χ at the stoichiometric mixture fraction Zst. Extinction depends on finite-rate chemistry and the specific fuel and conditions.

Damköhler number

τmix = δ²/D
Da = τmix / τchem

Da compares diffusion across the same illustrative layer with an assumed reaction timescale. Below 1, diffusion crosses the layer faster than the assumed reaction. Above 1, the opposite holds. A real extinction threshold requires a specific flame and chemistry model.

How this prototype works

Project Max Q searches a curated collection using topic matching and a visible relevance score. Its default answers assemble catalogued results and their limitations. Eligible browsers can also draft an optional on-device AI synthesis from the retrieved records.

Flight microgravity provides a reference for surface habitats. Lunar and Martian gravity, habitat geometry, atmosphere, and airflow require separate validation before application to mission hardware.
